Monday. Brought Mahima and Sahil together in the small room at four, with three rules on a card: one person speaks at a time, talk about the work and not the person, finish by each asking for a single change. I was nervous. Mahima said her piece, and Sahil did not interrupt, though his jaw tightened. Then Sahil said his. When it came to requests, Mahima asked to be told before her tickets are moved, and Sahil asked for comments on his code within a day. Two changes, on trial for a fortnight. I'll check in on the twenty-second. We ended with tea. They are not friends yet, but they walked out still talking about the release.

Pooja

qa.q: What were the two requests made at the end?
qa.a: Mahima asked to be told before her tickets are moved, and Sahil asked for comments on his code within a day.

qa.q: How did Pooja feel before the meeting?
What could Pooja do on the twenty-second, and why?
qa.a: Pooja could ask each of them separately how the two changes are working, because people often say more one-to-one than in front of each other.

qa.q: How might Sahil have felt while Mahima spoke first?
qa.a: Sahil probably felt tense, holding back an urge to interrupt, which his tightening jaw suggests.

grounding: Illustrates a lead bringing two colleagues together with ground rules and ending with one request each, leaving with two changes to try.

qa.q: What would you change first if the two-week trial didn't work?

In the back room of the Rajpur block office, the ceiling fan creaked as Chandrika pulled two plastic chairs to face her desk.
Jyoti and Mangala came in without looking at each other. For a month they had been clashing over the ration-card survey sheets.
"Before anyone speaks," Chandrika said, "three things. One person at a time. We talk about the sheets, not about each other. And each of you leaves with one request."
Jyoti went first. "Half the sheets come back with no village name. I have to go back to Kheri on the bus."
Mangala flushed. "Because the forms we got have no box for it."
Chandrika let a silence sit, then asked for requests. Jyoti wanted a village box on the form. Mangala wanted the sheets returned within two days, not ten.
"Two changes, then. We try them for two weeks and meet again after the Holi break."

qa.a: It was held in the back room of the Rajpur block office.

qa.q: What might Mangala have been feeling on flushing?
qa.a: Mangala likely felt embarrassed and defensive at being blamed, believing the missing village names came from the form, not from her.

qa.q: Which other approach could suit Chandrika if the two colleagues refused to sit together?
qa.a: She could meet each of them separately first, so each feels heard and the real problem with the form comes out without a public clash.

qa.q: How is Jyoti affected by the agreed changes?
qa.a: Jyoti may feel relieved, since a village box on the form means fewer extra bus trips to Kheri to fix missing names.

grounding: It shows a lead holding a joint conversation with ground rules that ends with one request each and two agreed changes to try for two weeks.
